metadata.title: TEENAGE CAREER DEVELOPMENT IN ENGLAND: A REVIEW OF PISA 2022 DATA

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The paper uses OECD PISA 2022 microdata for England and compares results to OECD averages. PISA employs a complex, stratified sampling design with school-level clustering and matrix sampling for career-development items, so analyses should use PISA-provided sampling weights to obtain population-representative estimates for 15-year-olds in schools. The manuscript notes that matrix sampling was used to reduce student burden (each question answered by about 1 471 students on average), implying that analysts should apply the appropriate PISA weights for the relevant matrix/booklet items when estimating participation rates and related indicators. The report does not describe any replicate-weight procedure (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so standard errors should be computed using the variance estimation approach recommended for PISA 2022 in the OECD technical documentation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This is a review/synthesis report using PISA 2022 descriptive statistics and cross-tabulations (e.g., participation rates, proportions by ESCS quartile, and comparisons to OECD averages), rather than an empirical model that explicitly reports how plausible values (PVs) were combined. While PISA includes PV-based achievement domains, the paper’s reported outcomes are career-development engagement and perceptions (and related categorical constructs), for which PV handling is not the central analytic step described in the text. Missing-data handling is therefore not documented at the level of an ML/achievement-PV modeling pipeline, representing a reporting gap for methodological transparency.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2022 data for England, with responses from 4 763 students in 165 schools. The paper indicates that PISA 2022 used matrix sampling for the career-development questions, so the analytic base for each career-development item/indicator is restricted to students who responded to the relevant matrix/booklet question(s) (average of 1 471 students per question). The report also cautions that the England sample may be somewhat over/under-representative on attainment and free-school-meal eligibility relative to the general population, but it does not describe additional exclusion rules beyond the PISA sampling and matrix design.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report reviews teenage career development in England using PISA 2022, focusing on students’ engagement in career-development activities, career thinking (e.g., career certainty, ambition, and misalignment), and perceptions of preparation for adult life. It compares England’s results to OECD averages and disaggregates patterns by student characteristics including gender, ESCS (socio-economic background), academic proficiency, migrant status, geographic location, and school type. The report finds that England performs well relative to many OECD peers on several engagement indicators, but that only 22% of students report participating in all three core activities by age 15 (workplace visit, job fair, and speaking with a career advisor), and that engagement gaps persist by ESCS. It also reports that career uncertainty and misalignment remain substantial—e.g., 27% of students in England are categorized as misaligned in 2022—and that career expectations align poorly with labour-market demand, with a concentration in professional occupations exceeding actual UK workforce shares. Methodologically, the analysis is descriptive and includes regression analysis, but the excerpt does not provide ML model performance metrics or PV/missing-data handling details for an ML pipeline.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD review/report that synthesizes PISA 2022 descriptive statistics and some regression analysis rather than training/evaluating machine-learning predictive models. Consequently, there are no ML algorithms to extract, no PV-combination strategy for an ML achievement model, and no ML-style target-variable performance metrics. The absence of explicit sample-size breakdowns by additional countries is consistent with the report’s focus on England while using OECD averages for comparison.
